title: Manchester City transfer news: Squad overhaul from a 650,000-strong database
description: Inside the confines of Manchester City's sophisticated data operation is a fundamental phrase its experts work towards: "What does it take to win?"In
body: Inside the confines of Manchester City's sophisticated data operation is a fundamental phrase its experts work towards: "What does it take to win?"In practice, the motto is broken down into three sections: identifying players, evaluating them and assessing how the club could improve them, all with a view to enhancing the statistical probability of City winning the Premier League.Last season, the club's data department projected they would be there or thereabouts when it came to the title race, but their metrics indicated Arsenal were favourites to be champions. They were accurate.This time around, City prefer to keep their projections under wraps - but five wins from five Premier League games have prompted predictions from supporters and pundits they will again be the Gunners' closest challengers.City's devotion to data is at the heart of their efforts to close the gap on Arsenal and BBC Sport has been given unprecedent access to the inner workings of the club's metrics machine as we uncover some of the secrets guiding their work - particularly regarding player recruitment and sales.Their work is a sign of the times in the Premier League, with clubs across the top flight and beyond increasingly using data for transfers and monitoring their teams' performance.At City, one of the fundamental aims is to reduce risk of any market transaction, be it a purchase or a sale.City grade players based on:Ability;Overall characteristics;The system they play in at their current club and how the manager is asking him and the team to play.Once those four aspects are observed, City's aim is to understand not just how good the player is but how good he could become at the Etihad.Since winning the Treble in 2023, City's squad has undergone a vast overhaul using this approach. Only four players from that historic campaign remain.It is crucial to stress, however, that while data has made an indefinite impact on how City operate in the transfer market, the work of traditional scouts continues to be the primary gauge of whether they decide to move for a player."Data plays a role in our decision-making, but it is just one part of the overall picture," City sporting director Hugo Viana told BBC Sport."We know data cannot tell us everything about a player. It cannot fully show a person's character, mentality or behaviour."That is why we study data insights but focus on the expertise of our scouts and other specialists."The prominence of data, however, has grown significantly behind the scenes at the Etihad. Here BBC Sport can take you to the core of some of City's key transfer calls from their extensive three-year squad revamp  - including the £116m signing of Elliot Anderson.The starting point for any new signing is City's database of 650,000 footballers from around the world.The next step is the brief: what sort of player is the club wanting to recruit. This usually starts with a position, though that process isn't as simple as it sounds.City, for example, categorise their full-backs into three types: those who are defensive, those who come inside, and those who play high and wide.Once the club's data departments have the brief, filters that grade a player's overall ability are applied to whittle down the 650,000-man database to 20-50 names.Juventus full-back Andrea Cambiaso is one player who has been on City's radar after the data highlighted him, particularly his ability to coming inside to build play in midfield.That he is comfortable with both feet rated highly on the data, too.In accordance with the data and the scouting reports it was decided the club would not proceed with their interest in Cambiaso in the previous window, but City's approach is likely to mean he will continue to be monitored.The longlist of 20-50 names is cross-referenced with the scouting longlist. Generally there is a significant overlap between the players identified by data and the ones already on scouts' radar.From there, further, more refined metrics are applied to rank and prioritise the longlist.Scouts will then complete further diligence on the players to reduce the list to a maximum of about six players.At this point, the club will complete deeper dives into the remaining players, including diligence on their injury record, athletic performance and behavioural habits.The information is then collated into individual reports called acquisition packs which contain all the key metrics used to inform the decision on a player.This includes a 'radar chart', which rates a range of specific on-field metrics.For example, when Jeremy Doku was signed in 2023, then manager Pep Guardiola decided he wanted a winger who was direct, akin to Leroy Sane, because at the time they had Jack Grealish and Riyad Mahrez, who preferred to keep the ball and cut inside.Among the criteria applied in City's brief were the following: making (running into) the box, pressure regains, take-on percentage and opposition-half pressure.Doku's overall numbers ticked the boxes Guardiola was looking for, although the Belgian's 'making the box' score was among his lowest readings.Since his arrival, Doku has improved this rating - an example City say shows how their data systems are helping to improve existing players.There is also a 'utilisation chart' that records how often the player has been used over a three-year period, as well as a scouting grade that indicates how highly the traditional scouts rate the individual.Each player is also awarded an overall "current impact score" - which predicts what impression he would be expected to make immediately on signing - and a "potential impact score" that projects the contribution the player could make in the future.Perhaps the most intriguing reading on the acquisition packs is a player's "action value score". This positions them in a league table that includes City players and ones from rival clubs who play in a similar role.Once the acquisition reports are evaluated, the list is further reduced to 2-3 players once City's valuation of the player has been factored in.Data contributes heavily to the price range City believe a player falls in, and the valuation is never a single number.A decision is then made on which player is the priority, though all players on the shortlist are worked on simultaneously in the event of changing circumstances, for example if a player becomes unavailable.Indeed, being able to move according to the market is something the data team feel they have become adept at.The sudden emergence of Yan Diomande last season led to City completing checks on him before he joined Real Madrid from RB Leipzig.The club also paid close attention to Eduardo Camavinga's metrics in case Real decided to sell a midfielder.Anderson was an obvious signing for a top Premier League club.The 23-year-old had developed into a key player for Nottingham Forest. An added appeal was the fact he is English, and had cemented his position in the national team.City fought off other top clubs, including Manchester United, to sign him.It would seem, on the face of it, a straightforward decision.But the way City analysed it underlines their incredibly forensic approach even when, outwardly, it might be considered they did not need to be so comprehensive given Anderson's obvious talents.The fact they still used their algorithm and went through all their normal steps says a lot about elite football in the modern day - and also the limitations of data alone.That is because - perhaps surprisingly - Anderson's metrics didn't necessarily catch the eye.At the start of last season, despite emerging uncertainty over Guardiola's future, the club knew they would be in the market for at least one central midfielder come the summer.They knew Bernardo Silva was leaving while there were doubts over the futures of Rodri and Nico Gonzalez.There was an acknowledgement that replacing Silva and Rodri like-for-like would be virtually impossible, so they looked for a player who was equally adept at building play from either deep or high central midfield.As last season developed, doubt also emerged over the future of Tijjani Reijnders - but Enzo Fernandez was viewed as the favoured replacement for the Dutchman.Anderson made the initial cut from the 650,000-man database to the longlist - but was not high in that group. However, his metric readings didn't immediately scream out the "no-brainer" he ultimately became.As City took a closer look, there was an acknowledgement Anderson's case does highlight some of the limitations of data.Anderson did not score lots of goals for Forest, or consistently provide assists. Because, generally speaking, Forest aren't a possession team like City, his general metrics in their algorithm did not grab the attention.With that in mind, City's data analysts had to consider that, because Anderson was generally playing closer to his own goal than he would at City, he wasn't getting the opportunities to impress in the final third of the pitch.So they paid close attention to what he was doing at Forest and modelled his potential role in a City team that generally plays closer to the opposition's goal,  dominates possession and has more elite players.Among the criteria graded on Anderson's 'radar chart' were defensive regains, duel success, line-breaking passes, aerial-duel success and defensive errors.With his reading for defensive errors, it was acknowledged that, because Forest were a transitional side, some were a result of the area of the pitch in which he was asked to operate.He may, for example, have regained possession deep inside his own half but lost the ball because he had to play a longer and a riskier pass after being asked to play forward quickly.In the same scenario at City, it is anticipated Anderson would have options to play a shorter pass with a greater success rate."Just because a player doesn't have the opportunity to perform a particular action on a regular basis because of the team he is playing doesn't mean he can't do it," said a source.Anderson's data readings improved significantly as the season developed, which compelled the club's scouts to watch him on a regular basis.He stood up very favourably against City's existing midfielders - and a list of rival players the club had identified as possible signings in that area.The results of the diligence completed by City's data team, scouts and other experts meant that even though Anderson's price increased beyond what City believed was his true valuation, they felt the risk was low."Elliot Anderson is a great example of how the process works," Viana said."The data was positive for Elliot and gave us real confidence in his profile, but it was the insight from our scouts and wider performance team that helped us understand the player and his attributes and this proved our belief that he was the right fit for the club."BBC Sport was also provided with fascinating insight into how data was used to sign Julian Alvarez from River Plate for £14m in 2022.The initial recommendation came from scouts, and given Alvarez was not a player originally identified by his metrics, the data team had to take a closer look.Because the Argentine league isn't recognised as one of the strongest globally, City's general data settings mean players will reach a natural ceiling with their readings in comparison to those playing in one of Europe's top five divisions.So, City dug deeper into Alvarez's stats, and his impact on both the ball and River's scorelines.The stats showed he was by far the best player in the Argentine top flight, and City believed they had enough evidence to say he would develop into a starter for a top-half club in one of Europe's top five leagues within two-and-half years.The data model valued Alvarez between £26m and £40m. City signed him for £14m so believed they were signing an undervalued player.Alvarez's projected value was £70m after three years. They eventually sold him to Atletico Madrid in 2024 for £81m.The signing of Abdukodir Khusanov from Lens also provides intriguing insight into City's reliance on data.The 22-year-old didn't initially make City's 50-man longlist, but on closer inspection they found while his output on the ball needed to improve, his physical data - for example his covering runs behind - was through the roof.Khusanov's on-the-ball metrics, City say, have improved significantly since he signed in January 2025.The departure of Guardiola and the arrival of Enzo Maresca is not expected to alter the club's approach significantly.The key metrics Maresca looks for in a player are understood to be very similar to Guardiola's, with the notable difference that the Italian prefers his full-backs to be more direct.Rooted in City's coach recruitment process is a certain team philosophy and way of playing, with any new manager expected to produce a side that is possession dominant, can press high, regain possession high up the pitch, produce quality chances and entertain.That philosophy was designed before Guardiola's appointment, and the Spaniard produced the purest form of City's footballing ideology.With that in mind, the change in manager has not drastically altered the way City's data department approach their work.Maresca will continue to work closely with them as he looks to build his own dynasty - but much of the hard work in building a squad to last is complete.Before City's Treble-winning season, the internal data indicators were such that the club knew they would soon need to overhaul a squad that had reached its peak.Selling players such as Kevin de Bruyne, Kyle Walker, Riyad Mahrez and Ilkay Gundogan wasn't easy given their illustrious service and the fact they were still performing at a very high level.Data, though, allows the club to spot declining trends well in advance - often two or three years - before a player is offloaded.Those particular metrics help City identify when the right time is to sell a player is - perhaps even before the buying club have spotted a drop in performance.And when those trends are identified, the club can plan well in advance.From there the club decide whether to start embedding a player from the academy or enter the market to replace.Ayyoub Bouaddi's arrival from Lille this summer is a prime example. At 18, City realise he isn't necessarily going to have a profound impact this season - but the club believe the Moroccan will be able to make a bigger contribution within two years.After the Treble season, the recruitment remit at City was to lower the average age of the squad and build a set of players that could deliver sustained success.But doing that at City comes with a catch. Because at City, the team are always expected to compete for trophies.Lowering the age of a squad is one thing; doing so while continuing to win is far more complicated.In previous years, for example, City's data systems identified former Brighton trio Moises Caicedo, Marc Cucurella and Carlos Baleba, who have been lauded as data successes.But there was a sense at City that the development of such signings would take too long for them to make an impact on a team that has the remit of winning titles or assets that could be developed and sold for a profit.City have successfully lowered the average age of the squad to the extent they now have the third youngest set of players in the Premier League behind Newcastle and Chelsea.But with the signings of goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, defender Marc Guehi, and Fernandez and Anderson they have added players who can not only grow with that new generation but also already have vast experience of top-level football.City's data indicates their current squad will not peak for another two to three years - but also projects they are likely be among the title challengers this season.Time will tell if they are right.

schema.headline: Manchester City transfer news: Squad overhaul from a 650,000-strong database

title: Andy Carroll: Former England striker reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021
description: Former England striker Andy Carroll has revealed he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021.The 37-year-old, who was automatically granted anonymity a
body: Former England striker Andy Carroll has revealed he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021.The 37-year-old, who was automatically granted anonymity as a victim of sexual assault, has made the details public in an autobiography titled 'Owning it'. The incident took place at Carroll's home, during his second spell with his hometown club Newcastle and led to the perpetrator being jailed for three years. Carroll, now a player/co-owner of non-league club Dagenham & Redbridge, says he decided to include the incident in his book "at the very last minute" after discussing it with his girlfriend Lou Teasdale.A friend of his former partner, who was away at the time, was set to stay over after coming to his home to watch a boxing match.Carroll says the incident occurred while he was sleeping and he then threw the man out of the house, before knocking him unconscious as he tried to return.Carroll, who also played in the Premier League for Liverpool and West Ham, called the police and was "sobbing" in the arms of his children's nanny.The unnamed attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and placed on the sex offender register. Carroll testified in court, a process he says was "humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous".Carroll wrote: "I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now."Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet."Scary to talk about but it's made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it."Carroll, who won nine England caps, added: "What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I'd think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football… The trauma of what happened to me hasn't gone away."Carroll joined Dagenham in July 2025 and has made six appearances in the National League South this season.If you have been affected by any of the issues in this article, you can find information and support at BBC Action Line

title: 105-year-old investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp in Germany
description: German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war c
body: German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war camp in World War Two.The suspect is alleged to have been a camp guard at Stalag 326 VI K in Senne in northwestern Germany.A similar case had also been under way involving a second former camp guard at Senne, Dortmund public prosecutor Sonja Frodermann said in a statement.That suspect died a few months ago at the age of 99, she said.No further details about the two former guards have been made public, however the two cases highlight the difficulties faced by prosecutors who continue to investigate Nazi-era crimes, with most of the remaining suspects already dead.More than 5.3 million soldiers from the Soviet Red Army were held in German captivity during World War Two and half are thought to have died. Many of those who did survive were treated as traitors on their return home.But the PoW camp, or Stalag, at Senne was one of the biggest.One in three Soviet PoWs entering Nazi Germany between 1941 and 1945 went through the complex at Senne, according to the memorial site, and they often ended up doing forced labour in the wider region. Living conditions at Stalag were horrific, and prisoners faced appalling mistreatment and malnutrition.Of the 180,000-200,000 Soviet prisoners of war registered there, many died and tens of thousands are buried there. PoWs from France, Poland, Serbia and Belgium were also held at Senne.

schema.headline: 105-year-old investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp in Germany

title: Police arrest 36 in raids on Vietnamese crime gangs across Scotland
description: Police arrest 36 in raids on Vietnamese crime gangs linked to human traffickingImage caption, One of the targeted sites was a nail salon in GlasgowByS
body: Police arrest 36 in raids on Vietnamese crime gangs linked to human traffickingImage caption, One of the targeted sites was a nail salon in GlasgowByScotland home affairs correspondentOne of Scotland's biggest police operations has targeted a Vietnamese organised crime group linked to human trafficking and cannabis farms.About 300 officers took part in simultaneous early-morning raids, leading to the arrest of 36 people and the discovery of 14 cannabis-growing operations.In total, police searched or checked 47 addresses in Aberdeen, Dundee, Falkirk, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Ayrshire, Lanarkshire, Midlothian and the Scottish Borders.Police Scotland allege the gang is involved in "poly-criminality," including human trafficking, drug production, fraud, money laundering and organised immigration crime.The force says the activities first came to light after Vietnamese criminals were connected to 150 cannabis farms discovered in Scotland last year.Around 120 people had been arrested - so-called "gardeners"- and drugs worth £26m were seized.Subsequent inquiries linked a single Vietnamese crime group to about a third of the farms, with months of planning leading up to Wednesday's raids.Det Supt Stevie Bertram said: "This was by far the biggest human trafficking investigation that Police Scotland has ever run."We wanted to disrupt and absolutely cripple that organisation."We wanted to do it all in one day and I think it's been a huge success. Essentially, they won't be able to function."All of the targets of this operation have been arrested and they are the ones we believe are running that operation."Figure caption, The police operation targeted a group linked to human trafficking and cannabis farmsPolice Scotland officers arrested individuals in Birmingham as part of Wednesday's enforcement action, which was carried out with support from Home Office Immigration Enforcement and His Majesty's Revenue and Customs."We think the group runs across the UK and internationally," said Bertram."We've met with regional crime teams from up and down England and Wales and Ireland, to look at what's happening across the country."Officers from the National Crime Agency based in Hanoi have been liaising with the authorities in Vietnam.Image source, Police ScotlandImage caption, A large number of plants were found in a raid in DundeeThe addresses raided by the police included a tenement flat in Edinburgh's South Clerk Street, a five-minute walk from one of the capital's busiest police stations.Three rooms were crammed with plants growing behind tarpaulin screens under bright lights.A box of seedlings was discovered in the kitchen. There were signs of occupation, though no-one was in the flat when the police forced entry.In Dundee, a cannabis operation discovered in two neighbouring flats had been extended into a shared loft.The police will now try to establish whether the people arrested include victims of human trafficking."Vietnamese nationals are still the highest nationality that we see being exploited in Scotland" said Bertram."A lot of hard work and investigation will go on from today."We'll examine mobiles, data, paperwork to make sure that if there is a victim of human trafficking, they're quickly identified as a victim."

schema.headline: Police arrest 36 in raids on Vietnamese crime gangs across Scotland

title: Premier League Bermuda Triangle: Do stats back Brighton, Bournemouth, Brentford social media theory?
description: Is this really the Premier League's 'Bermuda Triangle'?Image source, BBC SportImage caption, How do Brentford, Brighton and Bournemouth fare against t
body: Is this really the Premier League's 'Bermuda Triangle'?Image source, BBC SportImage caption, How do Brentford, Brighton and Bournemouth fare against the 'big six'? ByPrudent NsengiyumvaBBC Sport journalistIt's the place where points are lost and never to be seen again, according to a popular social media meme.Draw a line from Brighton to Bournemouth to Brentford and back down to Brighton again and you will have formed the Premier League's very own "Bermuda Triangle".Those three clubs have developed a reputation for taking points off the traditional Big Six - Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham. Recent results have only fuelled the narrative and helped to push the tongue-in-cheek theory.On Friday night, Brentford beat Chelsea 3-0. Less than 24 hours later, Brighton outclassed champions Arsenal, albeit by the same scoreline - though it was a victory that could arguably have been even more emphatic had David Raya not produced a couple of smart saves.Bournemouth, meanwhile, pushed Liverpool all the way before falling to a gritty 1-0 defeat, with Alisson forced into a brilliant recovery stop to deny the Cherries an early opener.Those are the sort of performances that stick in supporters' minds and help explain why the theory has taken hold.But does the data back up the meme?To a point.Since the start of the 2024-25 season, Brighton have been the best-performing non-traditional Big Six side against Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Man City, Manchester United and Spurs, taking 42 points from 26 games - an average of 1.62 points per match.The Cherries are not far behind, collecting 35 points from 26 matches, or 1.35 points per game.Brentford, however, have taken 22 points from 26 matches, averaging 0.85 points per game. Newcastle (1.46), Nottingham Forest (1.46) and Aston Villa (1.38) have all matched or outperformed the Bees against the traditional Big Six over the same period.In other words, the clubs most commonly grouped together by the meme have produced very different levels of success against elite opposition.Brighton and Bournemouth have consistently taken points off the Premier League's heavyweights. Brentford's record is less convincing.In fact, the Opta data suggests Brighton are the main reason the theory has gained such traction.Since Fabian Hurzeler took charge, only Kenny Dalglish's Blackburn have recorded a better points-per-game return against the traditional Big Six among managers of non-Big-Six clubs with at least 10 matches.The popularity of the Bermuda Triangle idea may say as much about perception as results.When it comes to recruitment and spending, Bournemouth, Brighton and Brentford operate in a different world to the Premier League's biggest clubs. They cannot simply outspend Arsenal, Liverpool or Manchester City.That makes their victories more memorable. Upsets also tend to linger longer in the memory because they fit a familiar story: well-run clubs outperforming opponents with significantly greater resources.The meme is not entirely without foundation, although the evidence is considerably stronger for Brighton and Bournemouth than it is for Brentford.Brentford's overall record is weaker, although a series of eye-catching victories under Thomas Frank and now Keith Andrews have helped cement their reputation as a difficult opponent for elite clubs. And the start to this season has helped: their Chelsea success added to by an opening day 3-0 rout of Spurs. But the numbers do not support a three-club phenomenon quite as clearly as social media might suggest.If there is a Premier League Bermuda Triangle, Brighton sit firmly at its centre.The Seagulls' record against the traditional Big Six is not merely impressive by modern standards. According to Opta, it is one of the best any non-Big-Six club has produced in the Premier League era.The only catch is that the evidence points less to a triangle and more to one standout club, with Bournemouth providing strong support and Brentford helping to supply some of the moments that keep the theory alive.

schema.headline: Premier League Bermuda Triangle: Do stats back Brighton, Bournemouth, Brentford social media theory?

title: Azerbaijan Grand Prix: George Russell fastest in Thursday practice as Lando Norris says McLaren are 'miles off' the pace
description: Lando Norris said McLaren were "miles off" the pace after the first day's practice at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.The world champion has won two of the
body: Lando Norris said McLaren were "miles off" the pace after the first day's practice at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.The world champion has won two of the past four races, and would likely also have been victorious in the last race in Madrid had it not been for the unfortunate timing of a virtual safety car.McLaren were hoping for a step forward in Baku after introducing a significant upgrade package to their car.But Norris was sixth fastest, 1.484 seconds off the pace set by Mercedes driver George Russell, after the first day's running."We're up there," Norris said. "Relatively, we're in the position we expect to be in, but I'm 1.5secs off the pace, so pretty pants."We'll see what work we can do tonight but it's a little knife in the heart when you see how far off you are."McLaren are one of several teams to bring a major aerodynamic development to Baku, theirs focusing on revised bodywork shaping around the sidepod air inlets, engine cover, floor and diffuser.Chief technical officer Rob Marshall said: "We've introduced a significant upgrade this weekend and the initial data suggests the car is behaving as our simulations predicted, which is a positive starting point. However, it's clear we haven't yet unlocked its full potential."Russell headed both practice sessions, with the F1 weekend running unusually from Thursday to Saturday because it is Azerbaijan's national remembrance day on Sunday.The Briton led team-mate Kimi Antonelli by 0.552 seconds in the second session. Red Bull's Max Verstappen was Russell's closest rival in the first session, when Antonelli suffered a hydraulic failure, and third fastest in the second session.Antonelli's reliability problems also meant he missed the first half of the second session, and overall he had half the amount of running of Russell.The Italian, who leads the championship by a massive 81 points from Russell, said:  "We tried to do the max with what we had. Lost quite a few laps in FP1 and then missing half off FP2 is never ideal, especially in a street circuit."But overall I feel it was a good recovery. I feel quite good in the car. A few things to work on but looking forward to tomorrow."McLaren's rivals rejected the idea that they were struggling badly.Red Bull technical director Pierre Wache said: "Mercedes are quicker. McLaren looks a little bit quicker or similar to us."Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur said: "The McLaren was very quick but they never finished their lap."And Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord said he did not "think the gaps are representative".Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad had his second crash in consecutive race weekends in practice, clipping the wall on the exit of the tight chicane leading into the section around the castle.In the context of the day, the margin between the two Mercedes drivers is to be expected but Antonelli is likely to close in on Friday in the run up to qualifying.Mercedes spent the first half-hour of the second session finishing off the repair to Antonelli's car, which involved an engine change.That meant he had to go straight into his performance runs on the soft tyre, having missed set-up and development time at the end of the first hour and the beginning of the second.Verstappen was 0.4secs slower than Russell in the first session, and 0.827secs adrift in the second.Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were next, but more than a second off the pace.Hamilton said: "For some reason we're just lacking speed."Vasseur added: "(The drivers) were not very pleased with the balance so we have a lot of work to do to find a good solution for tomorrow."Behind Norris, Alpine's Pierre Gasly was seventh, ahead of the the second McLaren of Oscar Piastri and Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, who is competing again after missing three races because of a broken wrist.Williams and Audi were other teams with major upgrades, Williams' focusing mainly on reducing their car's weight.Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz were 16th and 17th fastest, the Spaniard saying he "felt a step forward as expected" but that he had suffered a "scrappy day" with issues with brakes."In general I felt a bit better with the car but it looks like we are a bit closer to the midfield," he said.Thursday practice results

title: £170 a bag? Protein users squeezed as prices soar
description: There are, however, early signs that the market is starting to adjust.Wholesale prices for high-protein whey have begun to level off over the past cou
body: There are, however, early signs that the market is starting to adjust.Wholesale prices for high-protein whey have begun to level off over the past couple of months, although they remain much higher than they were a few years ago.For now though, the higher prices aren't putting off Max."It feels like protein is so important now, a lot more than it used to be. It's pushed out everywhere," he says."If you're doing exercise and not taking any, you feel like you wouldn't be recovering properly."But for students like Evie, managing on a much tighter budget, it's a different story."It was affordable on my gap year [when she was working], but now I'm at university, I don't think I'll continue buying it. It's not a necessity right now," she says.Amarpreet says he will continue buying protein, but admits "it's becoming a luxury". He says £170 for a bag is too much for him, so he's switching to a cheaper brand, which he can get for about £100 a bag.

schema.headline: £170 a bag? Protein users squeezed as prices soar

title: Fury vs Joshua: Cardiff to host heavyweight fight on 11 December
description: Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will contest their long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.The bout,
body: Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will contest their long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.The bout, more than a decade in the making, will be broadcast globally on Netflix.BBC Sport understands the main event could take place in the early hours of Saturday morning in the UK, with organisers considering a late start to cater for audiences in the United States.Joshua and Fury will come face-to-face at a news conference in London on Wednesday, 30 September, as the build-up begins to one of the most anticipated fights in British boxing history."I am inspiring a generation," Joshua, 36, posted on Instagram. Fury, 38, is yet to comment on the announcement. The event is being promoted as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and UFC chief Dana White. "Two of the best heavyweights of this generation, finally in the ring together," Alalshikh said."This will be one of the biggest fights in boxing history. I am very happy to make this fight happen for the fans."The former two-time world champions had already signed contracts for the bout earlier this year, but the date and venue had yet to be confirmed.London's Wembley Stadium and New York's Madison Square Garden were the frontrunners to stage the fight, but both presented issues before Cardiff recently emerged as an alternative.The Principality Stadium has hosted late-night boxing before, including Joe Calzaghe's fight with Mikkel Kessler in November 2007, which began at 01:00 GMT.Welsh Rugby Union and Cardiff Council officials welcomed the fight, saying it would reinforce the city's reputation for staging major events and could bring a significant economic boost, although some operational details still need to be finalised.Joshua had been pushing for the fight to take place in the UK and has got his wish."Forever indebted to the UK public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn't have got this over the line without you," his promoter Eddie Hearn said.It is notable that White, who fronts Zuffa Boxing, is involved in the promotion."For more than a decade, boxing fans have been clamouring for the heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. Together, they bring 66 wins, 52 knockouts and multiple heavyweight world titles into the ring," White said."On December 11, two of the biggest heavyweights of this generation finally collide - and the winner will take a significant place in heavyweight history."There was no official statement from Hearn or Fury's promoter Frank Warren in the official news release sent by Netflix. Hearn had previously said he did not want White to be involved in promoting the fight.A major fight in Cardiff taking place in the early hours might seem unusual, but there is precedent for UK events being scheduled around American television audiences.Ricky Hatton's career-defining victory over Kostya Tszyu at Manchester's MEN Arena in June 2005 began at about 02:00 local time, allowing US broadcaster Showtime to show the fight on Saturday evening.Less than a year later, Welshman Calzaghe's unification fight against Jeff Lacy at the same arena was staged at a similar hour. Calzaghe's 2007 victory over Kessler in Cardiff was also influenced by the US television schedule.Mixed martial arts has gone even later. Michael Bisping's UFC title defence against Dan Henderson in Manchester in 2016 began deep into the night, with the fighters making their way to the octagon at about 04:45 local time.When the UFC returned to Manchester in 2024, the UFC 304 main card began at 03:00 BST - corresponding with its traditional 22:00 start on the US east coast, with Briton Leon Edwards fighting Belal Muhammad in the main event just after 05:30.The precise timing of Fury-Joshua has yet to be announced and promoter Eddie Hearn has played down suggestions it could begin as late as 03:00 GMT.A ringwalk around 01:00 or 02:00 GMT would place the fight at 20:00 or 21:00 respectively on the US east coast.For years, British boxing has debated who would win, watched negotiations collapse and wondered whether Fury and Joshua would ever actually share a ring.Now, finally, there is a date and a venue. It's happening.In many ways, the uncertainty of recent weeks was the Fury-Joshua story of the past decade in miniature. In 2020, the two camps agreed the basis of a two-fight deal. In 2021, contracts were signed for an undisputed heavyweight contest, only for Deontay Wilder's successful arbitration case to force Fury into a third fight with the American. Then, in 2022, Joshua accepted a 60-40 split to challenge Fury, but that attempt also fell apart.Joshua gets the British fight he wanted, organisers are given a stadium capable of staging a huge event in December and broadcasters can tailor it towards American audiences.There is also an intriguing subplot in White's involvement. While it does not necessarily tell us who wielded the most influence behind the scenes, his involvement underlines just how many powerful figures were involved in finally putting this fight together.What matters most for supporters is that Fury-Joshua will happen in Britain. There are some fights that are about more than purses, broadcast deals and site fees. This is one of them.British fans have followed every twist: the world-title wins, the defeats, the comebacks, the rivalries and, above all, the failed attempts to make this contest.Now they will have the chance to travel to Wales and say they were there. Tens of thousands will descend on the Principality Stadium for what will be one of the biggest nights British boxing has staged in years.And somewhere among them may be a youngster attending their first fight, watching two of Britain's most recognisable sportsmen make their walks to the ring and deciding they want to lace up a pair of gloves themselves.The fight may have arrived years later than many wanted but Fury-Joshua can still leave that kind of legacy.

schema.headline: Fury vs Joshua: Cardiff to host heavyweight fight on 11 December

title: 'I can't see it stopping' - Middlesbrough's young men on gangs
description: Inside Hemlington Boxing Club in Middlesbrough, music is drowned out by the sound of gloves hitting pads.For young men here, nights in the ring are fa
body: Inside Hemlington Boxing Club in Middlesbrough, music is drowned out by the sound of gloves hitting pads.For young men here, nights in the ring are far better than the alternative.Because outside, away from the bright lights of the gym, riders wearing balaclavas roar past on quad bikes in the darkness."You see it all the time," says Dylan, a 20-year-old who trains at the club."But I just can't see it stopping. The police can't really do much against it."Attention has turned to organised crime in Middlesbrough since seven people, including two police officers, were killed last month in a crash.A Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by officers travelled the wrong way along the A66 and collided head-on with a police car.For young men like Dylan, who knew one of the lads killed, there are worries about how easy it is to get sucked into a criminal way of life."You could walk around the corner and there's just a gang of lads stood there and they shout you over," he says.Dylan and other boxers tell BBC Newsbeat they blame a lack of safe activities and opportunities for young people in the area. He says getting into the sport has kept them away from gangs on the streets. "It stops you going down these bad tracks of crime, drugs, and what most of the lads my age are doing," he says."It's just not something I want to be involved in, really," says Dylan."I don't think anyone would, but some people just get forced down these routes."Alex, 21, has been training at Hemlington for just over two years."If I wasn't here I'd just be out with my mates, or I'd just be sat at home doing nothing," he says.For Alex, it's not hard to see how others end up spending their time out in the streets."Realistically, what are you going to do on a night?" he says."There's nothing to do. Everyone's just out and about, especially the kids."Alex says crime has become "normal" in the area."You can't hide from it," he says."People find it a game almost, recording things for TikTok. It's a 'catch me if you can'."Since the A66 crash, Alex says, his family has been telling him to "get out" of the area."You hear nothing good from Middlesbrough any more," he says. "It's just got a bad reputation."I wouldn't want to bring my kids up round here with all the stuff that's going on".James, 24, who recently moved away to Peterlee, about an hour's bus ride north, says he used to see "quite a lot" of gang activity."It might be drugs or knife crime or little petty things," he says. Cleveland Police has been criticised since the crash, and some residents previously told the BBC they'd "rather die" than dial 999 because their trust in the force was so low.James and the other boxers who speak to Newsbeat take a more balanced view when it comes to the police, but agree more work is needed to improve relations.The authorities need to "get to know the people more, understand the people more" to build trust, says James."I think the moment you relate to people, that's the moment you've opened the door to getting people's trust."Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller tells Newsbeat the aftermath of the A66 crash has been hard for the force, with "an incredible amount of grief" for the two officers who died.But, she says, the local area has been "portrayed in the national media in a way that we don't necessarily recognise"."We appreciate there are issues here. We know that there are things that policing needs to do, others need to do to make this area feel safer and be safer,"  she says.Fuller says a "minority" intent on causing harm "can have a real disproportionate impact on communities" and encouraged people to report problems.She says the area should "be grateful" for lads like those at the boxing gym who'd chosen to "walk away" and not get involved in crime."We hope that people will look out for each other, spot signs of when people are getting drawn into crime and report it to us so that we can help people."

schema.headline: 'I can't see it stopping' - Middlesbrough's young men on gangs

title: Crashed RAF jet 'steered away from houses' before pilots ejected on Anglesey
description: Crashed RAF jet steered to 'avoid built-up areas' before pilots ejectedFigure caption, Moment pilots eject as RAF jet crashes in AngleseyByRob ThomasR
body: Crashed RAF jet steered to 'avoid built-up areas' before pilots ejectedFigure caption, Moment pilots eject as RAF jet crashes in AngleseyByRob ThomasReporting fromAngleseyRowenna Hoskin and Miriam BarkerBBC WalesUpdated 3 hours agoAn RAF jet was steered to "avoid built-up areas" before two pilots ejected out of the aircraft, an air force commander has said.Gp Capt Gez Currie, Station Commander, said: "The aircraft would have been aimed in a direction that the pilot believed was open field, in order to avoid built-up areas and anybody on the ground."The Hawk T2 aircraft had been flying out of the RAF Valley station on Anglesey on Wednesday when it plummeted to the ground in nearby Pencarnisiog, narrowly avoiding homes.The trainee and an experienced professional, who parachuted out of their plane moments before it crashed, are expected to make a full recovery after they were treated for minor injuries.Hawk operations have been paused by the RAF as a "precautionary measure" while investigations into the crash are ongoing - the Red Arrows are included in the pause as the aerobatics display team use the T1.Figure caption, Gp Cpt Gez Currie, Station Commander of RAF Valley, said the pilots are with their families Currie said the pilots were in hospital being cared for and were with their families. He would not give personal details about them and said the investigation was in its early stages, adding "it's far too early to even suggest what has happened in this occasion".He said: "It was a trainee, with a highly experienced instructor on a routine sortie, across the Anglesey area."According to the Ministry of Defence, a sortie is "one mission, one complete trip". He added that in the two-and-a-half years as station commander, and in his 30-year career as an air traffic controller, "this is the first time I've experienced this".Eyewitness Ollie Zalot said he was initially concerned that people on the ground could have been hurt as the crash happened near buildings, while Anglesey councillor Neville Evans said he thought it had been a "very lucky escape considering how close" the crash was to a village and caravan park.Image caption, The RAF plane crash happened near PencarnisiogA video of the crash shared on social media on Wednesday appeared to show the two pilots ejecting from the aircraft before it nosedives and crashes in flames.Separate footage also showed a plume of smoke and flames rising from the rear of a jet as it rolled down the runway before the crash. As the jet climbed, the flames seemed to disappear. Mikey Kay, a BBC security analyst who also served in the RAF for 20 years, told the BBC that while it was too early to say, it was possible that the cause of the crash was not an engine failure.In a statement on social media, the RAF said: "Both pilots are doing well, they are in extremely good spirits and expected to make a full recovery."A formal investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident is now under way and, as a precautionary measure, the RAF has temporarily paused Hawk T1 and Hawk T2 flying operations."Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, Danni JonesImage caption, The two pilots were able to eject themselves before the plane crashedSlide 1 of 5, Two figures floating in the sky with parachutes, The two pilots were able to eject themselves before the plane crashedThe Hawk T1, and newer T2 versions are transonic, two-seat training aircraft used to train fast jet pilots.The Red Arrows, based at RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire, are included in the pause, however they were not due to fly again until Le Touquet Airshow in France this weekend in any event. It is not known when the restriction will be lifted.

schema.headline: Crashed RAF jet 'steered away from houses' before pilots ejected on Anglesey

title: Blood tests find high levels of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory
description: Blood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK.Th
body: Blood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK.The residents, from Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, have been told they could be at elevated risk of serious health conditions from the substance, known as PFOA.The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency over contamination of soils and locally grown food from the substance, which is a type of forever chemical - so-called because they do not easily break down.That investigation said high levels likely came from the nearby AGC Chemicals factory, which used it in their manufacturing processes until 2012.Sam Hammond and her husband, both from the village, have been told they were at increased risk of health impacts from PFOA. However, she told the BBC was more shocked by her son's result."When we opened the results...it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale. "I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific. Knowing that I've offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them - that's heartbreaking," she said.Residents previously asked the council to test their blood for the chemical. But according to the UK Health Security Agency, PFAS monitoring is not currently recommended because "tests are unlikely to provide clear information for individuals".Instead independent tests were offered by Manchester Metropolitan University, paid for by investigative journalists Watershed and Law for Change - which funds cases covering environmental issues.Forty-nine residents volunteered, and they were told their blood test readings on Wednesday.Andrew Molloy found out he was in the highest-risk category."I was half expecting it to be just normal," he said. "Because the investigation here has all been focused on - you're only really being at risk if you eat fruit and veg from the garden or grow your own eggs - which I don't."Andrew's home was built on land that used to be part of the factory. He underwent the tests because he was worried about persistent health problems in his family."One of the first things I'm going to do is take [the results] to my GP and at least get it on my record. They seem to refuse to do anything related to this, but now I have hard information and data," he said.Mario Panteli, who was visibly shaken by his results, which were among the highest, said it was "quite emotional, a shock". He added: "I bought a property, assuming that this is our forever home. I'm going to have to stop my children from going in the garden, front and back. I feel constricted, like I'm in a cage now."Dr David Megson, who carried out the testing at Manchester Metropolitan University, said the results made him feel sick."To me, it shows something seriously wrong has happened to that community in that area, that the levels were far higher than anything we would have ever expected to see in the general population."More than 100 residents, including those who had their blood tested, are now considering taking a group legal action against AGC Chemicals to claim damages for the contaminationSarah Moore, partner at law firm Leigh Day - which is representing some residents - said compensation could be sought for financial losses on residents' homes and the impact it has had on their use and enjoyment of the land.She said damages could also be sought "in relation to the health risks, which we now consider to be a significant issue as a result of the testing we've been doing locally".The case would be "groundbreaking in the UK," she added and would be the first time a community has brought a legal claim over contamination from forever chemicals in the country.Overseas, one of the biggest legal cases over PFOA contamination was in West Virginia, in the US, which was depicted in the 2019 film Dark Waters. In that case, DuPont and Chemours Co settled more than 3,500 PFOA lawsuits for a total of $671m (£526m). Both companies have always denied any wrongdoing.Dr Steve Hajioff, a specialist in public health, who was not involved in the Thornton-Cleveleys blood testing, said PFOA levels could have been even higher in the past, given the factory stopped using the substance in 2012 and it does break down over time.He said the levels measured in Thornton-Cleveleys are associated with elevated risks of serious health condition, but added: "If you increase the risk of something really rare, like kidney cancer or testicular cancer, by 30%, then the chances of an individual getting affected are still pretty low."Moore said she was representing residents in the community who were pregnant and worried about their children, as well as those who have families who were refusing to visit their homes over concerns about the risks."What we're looking at in Thornton-Cleveleys at the moment might be seen as something of an outlier. My worry is that it's the tip of the iceberg, it's just the beginning," she added.The researchers said further blood testing should be done in the wider community to understand the scale of the issue.A previous report into PFAS in Jersey recommended that residents with elevated levels should be offered treatment, including cholesterol-lowering medications and blood letting - a treatment where blood is gradually withdrawn from a vein, allowing the body to naturally replenish it.Wyre Borough Council, which is overseeing the investigation into the site, said: "We recognise that PFAS is an emerging area of scientific research and will continue to press for updated advice and guidance from expert health agencies on behalf of our communities as further evidence becomes available."

schema.headline: Blood tests find high levels of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory

title: Developer fined £1m after man killed by falling window
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Mick Ferris was a coach driver for Clarkes of London, and had been returning to his coach when the window pane fe
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Mick Ferris was a coach driver for Clarkes of London, and had been returning to his coach when the window pane fell A property developer has been fined £1m after a window fell from a luxury riverside penthouse in south London and killed a coach driver.Mick Ferris, 53, was crushed when the pane of glass weighing 130kg (20 stone) fell 26 storeys from The Corniche in Vauxhall on 2 October 2018.His wife Rachel Ferris told the sentencing hearing at Inner London Crown Court that her husband's death "could have been prevented", after it emerged that a window fell from the same development in August 2017, but the design was not substantially changed as a result.Mitigating for the developer St James Group Ltd, Prashant Popat KC said his client was "deeply remorseful and regretful".Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Luxury flats at The Corniche, on Albert Embankment, have previously been listed for sale at £3mThe father-of-two was hit by the falling glass as he returned to his coach on central London's Albert Embankment that morning.Specialist façade contractor Lindner Prater was also fined £300,000, after it and St James were found guilty of ignoring "foreseeable risks".Luxury architecture firm Foster + Partners and engineering consultants Wintech Ltd were cleared of the same charge.Judge Boyle said St James should have been more robust in "ensuring the critical safety component" of the window was "present and engaged".He added that Lindner Prater "should have done more to complete and document the risk assessment process".In addition to the fine, Judge Boyle ordered St James and Lindner Prater to pay costs of £125,000 each.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The window panel was roughly 85 x 190cm (2.7ft x 6ft) and weighed 130 kg (20 stone) Ferris said her husband's death was "so sudden" and "out of the blue".In a statement read out in court, she said: "If somebody had done something differently – anything – it would have changed our lives. We wouldn't be in this position."I know it wasn't just one person, but one person could have changed this."What those companies did killed my husband."The thought this could have happened to anybody is always with me. It could have been a child." She also told the court that 400 people attended her husband's funeral, and said "he is missed by so many it was unbelievable".At the time of the incident, television host and fellow West Ham fan James Corden paid tribute to Mick Ferris on Twitter, saying: "He was a huge West Ham fan and has passed away in the most sudden of circumstances."He added: "Tell your loved ones you love them today."HSE principal inspector James Goldfinch said: "The fact lessons had not been learnt from a near miss the year before makes what happened on that day all the more galling."For a window to fall once was quite extraordinary, for it to fall again was simply criminal."Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Drinking at football matches - would fans welcome it?
description: When UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on his trip to the United Nations in New York, he might not have been expecting a question about football
body: When UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on his trip to the United Nations in New York, he might not have been expecting a question about football fans drinking alcohol in grounds.Burnham firmly believes the law that prevents supporters from having a beer at their seat during a match is outdated. It's a position the Everton supporter has long held, and when asked was happy to reaffirm."I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination," said Burnham, who feels football fans are singled out compared to those of other sports and events.There is no suggestion this is about to become official government policy, and last year MPs rejected a Conservative amendment to the Football Governance Bill that would have forced ministers to launch a formal consultation on scrapping the rule.That was, of course, before Burnham returned to Downing Street.It is a complicated and divisive issue, about not just safety. But is it something that match-going supporters actually want?Drinking alcohol at football grounds in England and Wales has been strictly controlled since the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act was introduced in 1985.It was brought in to counter escalating hooliganism through the 1970s and into the 1980s.The ban impacts clubs in the Premier League down to the National League. While beer can be sold, it must be consumed in areas that do not have a view of the pitch.Yet fans who support teams in the National League North and South and below can drink alcohol around the pitch.The ban is more strict in Scotland, with a law in place since 1981 that alcohol is only available in hospitality areas and not for other fans.It was initially imposed following a riot during the 1980 Scottish Cup final between Rangers and Celtic at Hampden.However, attitudes have been changing in recent seasons.It was lifted as part of a pilot scheme last year, with several Scottish clubs selling alcohol in clearly defined, monitored areas of the stadiums. It started with lower-level clubs, eventually being extended to the Premiership.The Scotland national team joined the trial for the friendlies against Japan and Curacao earlier this year. It has been extended to games against Switzerland on 29 September and Slovenia next month.The Women's Super League in England has just completed two seasons of successful trials and the rule preventing drinking in the stands has now been removed by the league's governing company, WSL Football.The women's game is not governed by the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act, enabling the competition organiser to make the change.Is there support for the move within English football's corridors of power?Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in August the competition had not "got a specific view" and "we'd need to give it some really careful thought".The English Football League, however, issued a statement on Thursday that said it would be "receptive to discussions around reviewing the current legislation". It added member clubs had already provided "a mandate to lobby for appropriate reform" which had "not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding".The Football Supporters' Association has for some time backed changing the law.Like the prime minister, it considers it to be unfair on football fans."I think it is outdated," FSA chairman Tom Greatrex told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme."If you go to watch football in Germany or in other places around the world, then it's perfectly acceptable."It is civilised and appropriate. There's no reason why that shouldn't be the case for football fans, as it is for fans of rugby league, watching Oasis, or anything else that happens often in the same stadiums in the same seats."The FSA's position is that clubs should have the choice, in consultation with supporters, to sell alcohol. Clubs might want to offer it in all stands, others in designated areas, while a few might choose not to do so at all.Other sports offer designated alcohol-free sections, something that football clubs may wish to copy for some families and supporters who do not consume alcohol because of their religion. The FSA acknowledges this, but believes having the option to make such decisions is important.It believes relaxing the law would be more popular the further down the leagues you go, where alcohol sales could potentially provide a crucial additional income stream.The UK Football Policing Unit rejected the suggestion, arguing alcohol plays "a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour" and that "other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour" that football does.Yet for Greatrex, there is already proof police are not open to ideas through their previous opposition to safe standing. Before it was introduced four years ago, Mark Roberts, who has been the national lead for football policing since 2014, told the BBC it would make it "easier to throw missiles, engage in hate chanting, racism, sneak alcohol in, take cocaine"."[The police] were telling everybody that we couldn't have standing at football again, that it would jeopardise safety, " Greatrex said. "Actually, what we saw then was a controlled, managed pilot projects to get that re-established."There hasn't been the level of disorder that some of the police sources were saying there would be. I think  the police should have more of an open mind and engage in this in a sensible and mature way."For many match-going fans, however, the prospect of beer being thrown and potential anti-social behaviour outweighs the opportunity to watch a game with a pint.Dave, a Chelsea fan from Twickenham, told Nicky Campbell on BBC Radio 5 Live, that he was "100% against it"."Have a look at some of the footage you see on social media at Boxpark, for instance. A goal goes in and there is beer and lager thrown everywhere," he said."I don't want to go round stinking of other people's beer and there is a fashion among certain supporters to throw their beer everywhere."If people can't go without drink for a 45-minute period there is something the matter with them."Adrian, from Leicester, claimed it would be the "worst idea you could come up with"."There is enough trouble with other things in football, with the flares, drug taking and other things," he added. "You throw the alcohol in as well. Football is tribal whereas other sports they aren't."But Ryan, a Wolves fan in Banbury, said "a solution that suits everybody" is to provide designated areas for drinking in stands.Football is in the only sport in the UK which faces restrictions on the consumption of alcohol.Some of these sports have issues with alcohol-related and anti-social behaviour, but none have the same reputation as football.The restrictions differ around Europe.There is a strict ban in the top two divisions of Spanish football, where only alcohol-free beer can be sold outside of hospitality areas. It can, however, be taken to seats.In the German Bundesliga, there is no ban on drinking at your seat. So relaxed is the approach to alcohol at games that you will even find people selling bottles of beer from shopping trolleys outside grounds. In the Italian Serie A it is similarly as relaxed, though to a limit of 5% ABV. Some games which are designated "high risk" have sales suspended in and around the stadium.In France, the Evin Law was introduced in 1991 which is pretty much in line with Scotland, as far as football is concerned. Alcohol cannot be sold at any sports event, other than in VIP areas.

schema.headline: Drinking at football matches - would fans welcome it?

title: County Durham breast cancer failure bosses to review 4,500 more cases
description: NHS trust to review 4,500 more breast cancer cases after failingsFigure caption, Watch: Denise (pictured), Pam and other women describe how they were
body: NHS trust to review 4,500 more breast cancer cases after failingsFigure caption, Watch: Denise (pictured), Pam and other women describe how they were failedByDuncan Leatherdale and Sharon BarbourNorth East and Cumbria health correspondentUpdated 3 hours agoHospital chiefs in County Durham have agreed to review up to a further 4,500 breast cancer cases after failings including delayed diagnoses and unnecessary surgeries were found.Hundreds of patients suffered harm under County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust, according to a review of cases dating back to 2023.The BBC previously investigated the failings and has spoken to multiple women affected, including one who said she felt "mutilated" and the trust's mistakes were "absolutely unforgivable".Ahead of agreeing to expand the review to cases dating back to 2015, members of the trust's board offered "sincere" apologies for the failings and harm caused.At an extraordinary meeting of the board held in Durham, board chair Alison Marshall said: "I would like to offer a sincere apology to all the women and their families who have been affected by the failings in our breast services."I can't imagine the impact that has had."She said they could "not turn back the clock" but would be "open, honest and transparent" about the failings.Chief nurse Gill Hunt told the board concerns were first raised in 2015 after a "service reconfiguration" and loss of breast surgical trainee posts.Over the following years patients and bodies such as the Northern Cancer Alliance, Care Quality Commission and NHS England raised multiple issues, she said.The key "themes" included treatment "not aligned to best practice", excessive surgery and delayed diagnosis, she said.The trust's breast surgery lookback review began in April 2025 by examining cases between January 2023 and February 2025.Hunt said 538 cases had been reviewed so far with 321 having experienced some form of harm, including one death.Image source, CDDFTImage caption, The trust has been reviewing breast cancer care at its hospitals and services in County Durham and DarlingtonAbout 640 patients had also contacted a special helpline asking for their cases to be reviewed, the board heard.The review cost about £523,000 in its first year and involved nine reviewers looking at about 80 cases a month, the report said.The board agreed to extend the review by one year at a time back to 2015, which would encompass up to 4,500 further cases and take an estimated five years to complete.Hunt said the expanded review would "provide a proportionate and evidence-led clinical approach" in response to "emerging findings", while decisions would be "supported by clear clinical rationale and formal governance review".Other "important learning" to come out of the review so far was about how bosses should respond to concerns raised by patients or other agencies, Hunt said."We are committed to doing the right thing," she said. Breast Cancer Scandal: Exposing the HarmBBC health correspondent Sharon Barbour investigates a deepening breast cancer scandal in County Durham and hears from women whose mastectomies were unnecessary.Watch on BBC iPlayer nowChief executive Steve Russell said the trust was "incredibly conscious women and their families" had experienced "distress, uncertainty and harm".He said no apology could undo that but the trust would "support women who have been impacted" in any way possible.For example, some women who had undergone unnecessary mastectomies could be offered breast reconstruction surgery as they previously should have been, Russell said.He also said the trust was currently exceeding national standards for breast cancer treatment, including for the number of women having breast conservation surgeries and being offered immediate reconstruction."None of that changes what has happened to women in the past but hopefully gives confidence the changes made in the service have had an impact on the outcomes," Russell said.He said patients today could be "confident" they would be "treated appropriately" and get "good clinical outcomes".The helpline, which is available by phone or email, would remain open with any concerned patients encouraged to contact it "irrespective" of when they were treated, he said.Image caption, Denise was one of the women who had an unnecessary mastectomy  Denise Howarth attended the board meeting along with other patients.The 51-year-old from Consett, County Durham, who had an unnecessary mastectomy, said she was "pleased" the review would be extended as there could be many more cases still to be revealed.But past patients needed to be contacted with "dignity" and "compassion", she added, to try and reduce the "shock" and "pain" of being told their cases were being reviewed because of possible failings.She also said a public inquiry needed to be held and, as her case dated back to 2012, the trust's review should also look back further than 2015.Image caption, Rachel Gray contacted the trust's review helplineRachel Gray, 41 and from Sunderland, said she contacted the helpline after hearing of women "being harmed", with the review finding she could have avoided having a mastectomy at the age of 37.She said discovering that made her "want to crawl out of my skin".The board's decision to review more cases would mean there would be "more answers" and women finding out what had happened to them, she said.She also said she thought the review would find more women harmed "than what they are predicting".Medical negligence solicitor Chloe Gibson, who is representing women affected by the breast cancer scandal, said she welcomed the board's decision but warned the process would be "very long" and last until the 2030s.Waiting for their cases to be reviewed would cause "further anxiety and trauma" for many, she said, adding: "Justice delayed is justice denied."She also said the review should look further back than 2015 while a full public inquiry was the "only way proper scrutiny and full accountability can be achieved".Follow BBC North East on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external. Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story? If you feel able to do so, please get in touch.
